title: Mistakes at work

segments.voice: Yesterday, a difficult boss: Epictetus sees the other side, Benedict's monk speaks at a fitting time, Luqman remembers the sweet. Your line was calm under orders. How did the hardest instruction look from the other side? Day nine hundred twenty.

The report has already gone out to the whole team, and the totals at the bottom are wrong. Nobody has noticed yet. There's a small window, about the length of a coffee, when the mistake belongs only to its maker. It could be fixed quietly. It could be left to see if anyone spots it. Or there's a hard message to send, just three words long: that was me. Old texts from two very different places have something to say about that window. Today: Zigong.
screen: `THE TOTALS ARE WRONG.` → `A SMALL WINDOW.` → `THAT WAS ME.`

segments.voice: First, Proverbs, in the King James Bible: "He that covereth his sins shall not prosper: but whoso confesseth and forsaketh them shall have mercy." There are two moves after the mistake. Confess it: say it out loud. Forsake it: stop doing it. The thing that doesn't prosper isn't the mistake. It's the covering. Second, Confucius. In the Analects he says, more or less: to have a fault and not change it, that is what's really called a fault. The first slip is ordinary. Hands slip. The real fault, for Confucius, comes after, in the refusal to change. Third, his student Zigong adds a picture. A noble person's faults, he says, are like eclipses of the sun and moon. When he errs, everyone sees it. When he changes, everyone looks up to him. An eclipse doesn't hide. It happens in full view, it passes, and the light comes back where everyone can see it. Fourth, putting it to work. Own it, fix it, learn: the phrase is modern, but the old texts hold each step. Proverbs says confess, which is owning it. It says forsake, which is fixing it and not repeating it. Confucius says change, which is learning. At work, all of this can fit into two plain sentences. I got that wrong. Here's what I'm doing about it. No speech, no long account of why it wasn't really your fault. Just the eclipse, in full view, and then the light.
screen: `CONFESS AND FORSAKE.` · `THE REAL FAULT IS NOT CHANGING.` · `FAULTS LIKE ECLIPSES.` · `OWN IT, FIX IT, LEARN.` · then, large: `I GOT THAT WRONG.`

segments.voice: Sit comfortably and let the breath slow. Bring to mind one recent mistake, at work or at home. Nothing dramatic is needed. Notice what rises: the urge to explain, to soften, to make it smaller. Let that pass by. Now, silently, try the plain sentence: I got that wrong. Then name one small fix, and one thing you'd do differently next time. If there's someone who should hear the sentence out loud, let their face come to mind. If you pray, you can bring the mistake to God in your own tradition's words. The bell holds the time.
Zigong. Confucius's student who said a noble person's faults are like eclipses: seen by all, then lit again when changed. Today's word.
Your line: own it. Today, if a mistake of yours turns up, say so plainly and early, before anyone has to find it, and then set it right. Day nine hundred twenty.

howItsDone: Readers of the Analects return to its sayings on faults as a guide to self-correction, and Jews and Christians read Proverbs 28:13 as a call to confess wrongs and turn from them.

fork.setup: you're the noble person in Zigong's saying, and you've made a mistake everyone can see. what does he say happens when you change?
fork.reveal: like an eclipse: everyone sees the fault, and when it passes, everyone looks up.

original.note: Chinese, Analects 15.29: to err and not change, this is called a fault. 過 (guò) is the word for a fault.

trapdoor: what you thought: a mistake at work is something to hide until it blows over.
what it means: own it, fix it, learn: say it plainly, set it right, and change.
what a scholar hears: Analects 15.29, where the real fault is the one not changed, and 19.21, where a noble person's faults are like eclipses everyone sees.
